Article Title: Cloudflare Outage: Cloudflare goes down again: Users report facing issues with multiple apps
Article Text:
Global internet services faced disruptions as Cloudflare experienced a significant outage, impacting popular platforms like Zerodha and Canva. Users worldwide reported access issues. Cloudflare confirmed the problem, stating it was investigating and later announced a fix had been implemented. The company has since declared the incident resolved, restoring critical online functionalities.

Update: The company has confirmed that the outage has been resolved.

Cloudflare down: OpenAI, Twitter, Spotify, Canva, Claude and other big businesses that Cloudflare outage 'disrupted'

(Developing story)





Cloudflare’s services are experiencing another outage, with users worldwide reporting issues accessing multiple apps. The blackout is affecting several websites, including Zerodha, Canva and Downdetector, and has left many people unable to use critical online services. The company's service status page noted: "Cloudflare is investigating issues with Cloudflare Dashboard and related APIs. Customers using the Dashboard / Cloudflare APIs are impacted as requests might fail and/or errors may be displayed. We are continuing to investigate this issue."During the outage, the company said: "A fix has been implemented and we are monitoring the results. We are continuing to monitor the results."Cloudflare's status page also noted: "Scheduled maintenance is currently in progress. We will provide updates as necessary."The company's CTO Dane Knecht took to microblogging site X (formerly Twitter) to confirm:"We are aware of the issue impacting the availability of Cloudflare’s network.It was not an attack; root cause was disabling some logging to help mitigate this week’s React CVE. Will share full details in a blog post today. Sites should be back online now, but I understand the frustration this causes and the work being."During the outage several users also shared reports and memes about the latest Cloudflare outage. The outage affected apps like Canva, Zerodha and Groww.This is the second time in a month when the IT infrastructre company faced a major outage. Last month, the outage affected major platforms including ChatGPT, Spotify and US President Donald Trump's social media site Truth Social.Cloudflare is an important for the internet as it supports much of the traffic. It helps websites stay online during heavy traffic and protects them from cyberattacks. It sits between users and websites, improving speed and security. As many businesses depend on Cloudflare, even a single issue in its system can cause many unrelated websites to go down at the same time.
Article Summary: Users worldwide reported access issues. Cloudflare confirmed the problem and later announced a fix had been implemented. The company has since declared the incident resolved, restoring critical online functionalities. Last month, the outage affected major platforms including ChatGPT, Spotify and US President Donald Trump's social media site Truth Social.

Article Title: Researchers equip giant cockroaches with medical backpacks, fitted with cameras and syringes, the cyborgs search trapped survivors to deliver life-saving aid in disasters
Article Text:
Image credit: X (Twitter)

How these cyborg cockroaches work

What the tests reveal about the technology

How search and rescue teams could use them

Giant cockroaches could help rescue survivors after disasters. Researchers in Australia are developing cyborg-like insects equipped with miniature backpacks containing cameras, electronics and syringe systems designed to deliver emergency medication. The technology aims to help search-and-rescue teams locate injured people trapped beneath rubble and provide medical assistance when direct access is difficult.Called “paraborgs,” these modified insects combine their natural ability to navigate confined spaces with remotely controlled equipment. Scientists are testing whether the cockroaches can carry medical supplies into hazardous areas, identify potential victims through camera feeds and deliver drugs to targets. The approach could eventually support emergency responders dealing with collapsed buildings, earthquakes and other disasters where time and access are critical.According to a BGR report, the project involves researchers associated with the University of Queensland and the University of New South Wales. By combining insect movement with miniature electronic systems, the team aims to reach places conventional rescue equipment may struggle to access.The project uses the giant burrowing cockroach, scientifically known as Macropanesthia rhinoceros, a large cockroach species native to Australia. Its size makes it suitable for carrying a small electronic backpack containing a camera, control equipment and a syringe-based delivery mechanism.Unlike conventional robotic devices, these insects retain their natural ability to move through tight spaces. Researchers use implanted electrodes to stimulate the cockroaches' nervous systems, letting operators remotely control their direction. This could help guide them through gaps in collapsed structures and other areas human rescuers cannot easily enter.The cameras mounted on their backs provide a view of the surrounding environment. Rescue teams could use these images to assess obstacles, identify accessible routes and look for people who may be trapped nearby.The medical delivery system is another part of the design. Researchers have developed a mechanism that can fire a small syringe, described as functioning like a dart gun, towards a target. The aim is to deliver medication when a person needs urgent treatment and a medical professional cannot reach them immediately.Potential applications include delivering drugs to people experiencing certain emergencies, such as snakebite or severe allergic reactions. However, the technology remains experimental, and using it in real disaster rescue operations would require further testing.Early testing has examined whether the cockroaches can reach designated checkpoints and successfully deliver medication using the syringe mechanism.According to the reported results, the insects reached the checkpoints with a 100% success rate. The syringe system recorded a 72% success rate when delivering medication to targets. When the syringe was fired from within six inches of a target, the success rate increased to 95%.These results indicate that the insects can navigate designated routes under test conditions, while the distance between the syringe and its target remains an important factor in delivery accuracy.The findings also highlight the distinction between successfully guiding an insect to a location and delivering medicine accurately. In a real emergency, researchers would need to account for uneven terrain, limited visibility, unpredictable movement, and the injured person's condition.Further development would also be necessary to establish how the equipment performs in different environments and whether the system can deliver medication safely and consistently.Search and rescue operations often involve locating people in unstable buildings, collapsed structures and debris-filled areas. Sending rescuers into these environments can be difficult because of restricted access, falling material and the possibility of further structural collapse.Small insects equipped with cameras could provide another way to inspect such locations before a human rescuer enters. Their ability to move through narrow gaps could help teams gather information about spaces that are difficult to examine using larger equipment.Time is another consideration. Finding an injured person quickly can affect the treatment they receive, especially when the emergency involves a condition that requires prompt medical attention. Camera-equipped cockroaches could help rescuers assess a location and identify a possible route towards someone who needs assistance.The technology may also help reduce the physical demands placed on rescue workers. Rather than manually clearing every accessible section of debris, teams could first use the insects to inspect selected areas and determine where further intervention is needed.However, the system would not replace conventional rescue personnel or medical treatment. Its effectiveness would depend on camera visibility, remote control, access to the target, and the ability to safely deliver the appropriate medication.For now, the research demonstrates a potential application of biohybrid technology, which combines living organisms with electronic systems. If further testing establishes its reliability and safety, these cyborg cockroaches could become an additional tool for locating and assisting disaster survivors in places where conventional rescue equipment has limited access.
Article Summary: Researchers in Australia are developing cyborg-like insects equipped with miniature backpacks containing cameras, electronics and syringe systems. The technology aims to help search-and-rescue teams locate injured people trapped beneath rubble and provide medical assistance when direct access is difficult. Scientists are testing whether the cockroaches can carry medical supplies into hazardous areas.

Article Title: Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar ZP launches hand washing drive
Article Text:
Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar

:





The Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar zilla parishad (ZP) on Thursday will launch a mass hand-hygiene awareness initiative across gram panchayats, health centres, schools and anganwadis to mark Global Handwashing Day.Under the message “Wash hands, be a hero”, the ZP has appealed to these institutions to organise awareness activities and encourage residents to adopt handwashing as a regular habit. The initiative focuses on making hand hygiene a community-driven practice, particularly among children, the elderly and the rural population.“Washing hands with soap before eating and after using the toilet remains the simplest, cheapest and most effective shield against diarrhoea, stomach infections and respiratory illnesses among other ailments,” ZP president Avinash Galande said.“The ZP has directed BDOs, BEOs, taluka health officers and CDPOs to prepare taluka and village-level plans for demonstrating the 20-second handwashing method at PHCs, sub-centres, veterinary dispensaries, ZP schools and anganwadis,” women and child welfare chairperson Meenakshi Pawar said.The method involves wetting hands with running water, applying soap, scrubbing palms, between fingers, under nails and wrists for 20 seconds, rinsing and drying with a clean towel or air drying. Different local authorities have been directed that photo and video reports of the drives be submitted by Oct 20.
Article Summary: The Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar zilla parishad (ZP) will launch a mass hand- hygiene awareness initiative across gram panchayats, health centres, schools and anganwadis. The initiative focuses on making hand hygiene a community-driven practice, particularly among children, the elderly and rural population.

Article Title: An Arizona homebuilder spent years and hundreds of thousands of dollars turning his backyard into one of America’s largest private garden railways, with nearly 4,000 feet of track and hundreds of trai
Article Text:
Sirrine had been interested in model railways from a long time (Photo: All About Mesa AZ. Image enhanced by AI)

How an empty backyard became a railway

Electrical problems led to a different operating system

The features Sirrine's most proud of

An Arizona businessman who made his name in homebuilding and design spent years and hundreds of thousands of dollars turning his backyard into one of the largest private garden railways in the United States. Dennis Sirrine, began building the Palo Verde & Southwestern Railroad in January 2004. The project eventually featured nearly 4,000 feet of railway track and a collection of hundreds of model train cars.According to the PBS programme Tracks Ahead, Sirrine used his experience in construction to develop the large outdoor railway. The layout included winding tracks, artificial mountains, lakes and rivers, with sections raised several feet above the ground to make the trains easier to see.Sirrine had been interested in model railways from a long time. During his years as a general contractor, he sometimes incorporated railway layouts into the houses he designed. These involved installing wooden shelves near ceiling height, laying tracks on them and allowing model trains to travel through several rooms.His backyard railway, however, was a much larger undertaking. What began as an empty piece of land required extensive construction, repeated modifications and a complicated operating system.Sirrine told PBS that some parts of the railway had to be built more than once before he was satisfied with the results.When construction began in January 2004, Sirrine's backyard was largely flat, with no existing railway infrastructure. After studying garden railways elsewhere in the country, he decided that an elevated layout would provide a better viewing experience than tracks placed directly on the ground.The railway was therefore constructed at heights ranging from 30 inches to six feet. According to Sirrine, approximately 1,000 cubic yards of soil were brought onto the property to raise different sections of the layout.The raised tracks allowed visitors to watch the trains without having to bend down or kneel. Sirrine also designed the surrounding landscape to resemble real railway routes, incorporating changes in elevation, curves, lakes and rivers.His previous construction experience helped him undertake the project, but it did not prevent problems. Sirrine said he had worked in the construction industry for 17 years and understood the building process. Even so, several sections did not turn out as planned.He estimated that nearly half the layout had to be removed and rebuilt because of construction problems or incorrect advice about particular methods. Repeating completed work became one of the project's biggest challenges.Building the tracks was only part of the work. Sirrine also had to develop a system that could operate different types of model locomotives across the extensive railway.The original electrical arrangements involved approximately 1,000 feet of wire and 10,000 feet of conduit. Looking back, Sirrine said he would have preferred battery-powered trains from the beginning.The railway eventually used a combination of battery power and electricity supplied through the tracks. This arrangement also allowed visitors who owned electrically powered locomotives to operate their trains on his layout.Another major challenge involved the turnouts, or switches, which allow trains to move between different tracks. Sirrine had observed electrical switches developing corrosion and operational problems on other garden railways.Concerned about their reliability in Arizona's climate, he chose air-powered switches manufactured by the California and Oregon Coast Railway company in Oregon. The system operated using a compressor rather than relying on electrical switches.Sirrine told PBS that the air-powered system had worked reliably after installation, resolving one of the most difficult operating problems he had faced.Despite the project's size, Sirrine identified two particular achievements when discussing his railway with PBS- the accuracy of the tracks and the construction of the artificial mountains.The tracks were laser-levelled to keep them straight and ensure smooth changes in elevation. According to Sirrine, visitors had placed video cameras on flatbed railway cars and recorded their journeys around the layout. They were impressed by how smoothly the trains travelled.Meanwhile, the mountains required a different construction method. Sirrine used flat concrete panels designed to resemble rock, breaking them into sections before arranging, grouting and staining them to create realistic desert formations.The resulting landscape formed part of a railway designed to combine model trains with the appearance of natural terrain.
Article Summary: Dennis Sirrine began building the Palo Verde & Southwestern Railroad in January 2004. The project eventually featured nearly 4,000 feet of railway track and a collection of hundreds of model train cars. The layout included winding tracks, artificial mountains, lakes and rivers.

Article Title: OpenAI faces lawsuits from 8 US states over ChatGPT’s alleged harm to users
Article Text:
lawsuits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about ChatGPT’s safety

States seek changes to ChatGPT

OpenAI faces growing legal challenges

OpenAI is facing a fresh legal challenge in the US, with attorneys general from eight states accusing the company of exposing users, including teenagers, to harmful behaviour through its ChatGPT chatbot. The lawsuits allege that the AI tool has reinforced delusions, encouraged self-harm and helped users plan violence, including mass shootings.Attorneys general from Iowa, Kansas, Arizona, Arkansas, Idaho, Montana, Nebraska and West Virginia filed separate lawsuits in state courts on Wednesday. The complaints claim ChatGPT is designed to be agreeable and engaging to build users’ trust, potentially making them more vulnerable to dangerous interactions.The lawsuits accuse OpenAI of violating state consumer protection laws by misleading users about ChatGPT’s safety. They also allege that the company has created a public nuisance by endangering the health and safety of residents.The states are seeking court orders requiring OpenAI to change how ChatGPT operates. Among their demands is a prohibition on developing AI models capable of improving themselves unless the company can ensure that the models are aligned with human values.The states are also seeking civil monetary penalties for alleged violations of state laws, along with damages.The coordinated legal action adds to mounting legal scrutiny of OpenAI as the company prepares for a potential public listing. It represents a significant coordinated effort by state authorities to challenge the safety of an AI company’s products.Florida’s attorney general filed the first lawsuit of its kind by a US state against OpenAI in June, citing concerns over child safety.The company is also facing dozens of lawsuits brought by private plaintiffs alleging that ChatGPT contributed to harmful behaviour, including helping users plan mass shootings and other acts of violence.
Article Summary: States seek changes to ChatGPT. OpenAI faces growing legal challenges in the US. Lawsuits allege that the AI tool has reinforced delusions, encouraged self-harm and helped users plan violence, including mass shootings. Florida’s attorney general filed the first lawsuit of its kind by a US state against OpenAI in June.

Article Title: In Cameroon’s black-cotton-soil road experiment, researchers mixed bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime into the ground; its bearing score rose from 2.7% with bamboo charcoal alone to 19% with the fi
Article Text:
Representative AI image of workers mixing bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime into black cotton soil to strengthen a rural road in Cameroon. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

Why Black Cotton Soil creates problems for roads

How quarry dust and lime improved the mixture

Bamboo charcoal made by NARO Uganda. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Could the mixture be used in road construction?

Building durable roads on weak soil is costly, particularly in regions where the ground swells when wet and shrinks as it dries. In Cameroon, researchers tested whether bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime could strengthen Black Cotton Soil, an expansive soil that can weaken road foundations.According to a study published in the International Journal of Civil Engineering , the researchers examined how combining the three materials affected the soil’s load-bearing capacity. The best-performing mixture, containing 20% bamboo charcoal, 12% quarry dust and 5% lime, increased the soaked California Bearing Ratio (CBR) from 2.7% to 19%. The laboratory results suggested that the combination could improve the suitability of this difficult soil for road construction, although its performance under actual road conditions would require further assessment.Black Cotton Soil contains large amounts of clay and changes volume as moisture levels vary. In wet seasons, Black Cotton Soil absorbs moisture and swells. When it dries, it tends to shrink and form cracks. These changes can strain road foundations and deform the road surface. The problem is especially serious when the subgrade, the prepared earth beneath the road, is made of Black Cotton Soil.The research explains that bamboo charcoal was first used as a soil amendment to alter the soil’s engineering properties. The researchers tested several charcoal proportions and selected the 20% bamboo charcoal mix for further analysis. The selected mixture achieved only a 2.7% soaked CBR. That led the researchers to test other substances that could improve the mixture. Lime and quarry dust were added in sequence to enable the scientists to observe the impact of each substance on the bearing capacity of the soil. This approach matters because soil stabilisation involves more than simply adding one material to the soil.Quarry dust is a fine material produced during rock crushing. When added to the bamboo-charcoal-treated soil, it helped improve the mixture’s bearing capacity. The addition of lime produced a further increase, bringing the soaked CBR to 19%, more than seven times the value recorded for the charcoal-only mixture. The researchers also found that the soil’s Plasticity Index fell to 11.2%, indicating a reduction in its plasticity.These results are consistent with other studies on stabilising expansive soils. A study published in Construction Materials found that chemically stabilising black cotton soil improved its engineering properties, highlighting the importance of selecting suitable additives. However, the Cameroon experiment’s results came from laboratory tests and do not guarantee the same performance on construction sites, where soil composition, drainage, rainfall and compaction can vary. Further field testing would be needed to establish how reliably the mixture performs under real road conditions.The Cameroon experiment was notable for combining three materials to improve the strength of difficult soil. Bamboo charcoal offered a potential use for processed bamboo, while quarry dust provided a way to reuse a by-product of stone processing. Lime, already used in soil stabilisation to modify plasticity and improve soil properties, formed the third part of the mixture. The significance lay in testing how these materials worked together, rather than assuming that any one additive could deliver the same results on its own.For road builders, the approach could be useful in areas where expansive soils are common and conventional ground improvement is expensive. However, its practical value would depend on the cost of producing and transporting bamboo charcoal, the local availability of quarry dust and the amount of lime required. The environmental impact of charcoal production would also need to be considered.Further field trials would be necessary to establish how the treated soil responded to repeated traffic loads, wet and dry cycles and changing groundwater levels, as well as whether the mixture could be prepared and compacted consistently at construction sites. Although the researchers reported a substantial increase in bearing capacity under the tested conditions, its performance and cost-effectiveness in wider road-building applications would require further assessment.
Article Summary: Researchers tested whether bamboo charcoal, quarry dust and lime could strengthen Black Cotton Soil, an expansive soil that can weaken road foundations. The best-performing mixture, containing 20% bamboo charcoal and 12% quarry dust, increased the soaked California Bearing Ratio from 2.7% to 19%. The laboratory results suggested that the combination could improve the suitability of this difficult soil.

Article Title: In 2002, Japan widened a 70-metre road using crushed oyster shells in its base; testing found the shell section exceeded the ground improvement target
Article Text:
Representative AI image of road construction using crushed oyster shells mixed into the road base, with workers and machinery compacting the material to strengthen the surface. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

Why Japan was looking for a use for discarded oyster shells

What happened after vehicles began using the road?

In a unique study, researchers in Japan explored the application of crushed oyster shells for enhancing the structural integrity of roads in a widening project. Image credit: Wikimedia Commons.

Could seafood waste become a regular road material?

Discarded oyster shells are often associated with seafood waste, stockpiles and the challenge of finding storage space. In parts of Japan, oyster-farming shells became the focus of a practical engineering experiment. Rather than sending the material for disposal or using it only in agriculture, researchers investigated whether crushed shells could help strengthen the ground beneath roads.According to a study published in the Journal of the Society of Materials Science , Japan, crushed oyster shells were tested in a Japanese road-widening project in March 2002, with the trial covering a 70-metre stretch. Researchers monitored the road’s response to traffic using pavement deflection measurements and found that deflection decreased over time. The section containing nearly dry oyster shells also achieved an estimated California Bearing Ratio above the target set for ground improvement. The findings suggest that discarded oyster shells may be useful for strengthening road subgrades, although further testing is needed under different conditions.The experiment aimed to address a practical problem in oyster-producing areas.After oysters were removed, the shells would pile up in storage yards. Some of these would be used again as an additive to animal feeds, fertilisers, and soil conditioners. This method of using shells did not always keep up with production levels. Piling up shells caused problems in terms of occupying space and creating foul odours and worsening the environment. Using these shells for crushing purposes presented an alternate solution. The crushed shells would be used for making better roads.The approach was not entirely untested. A study published in Doboku Gakkai Ronbunshu in September 2002 examined the suitability of crushed oyster shells for road subgrades through laboratory experiments and simulated ground-improvement tests. The researchers found that incorporating roughly 20% crushed shells could improve the ability of construction equipment to travel over the treated ground and could contribute to the effectiveness of soil stabilisation. The study suggested that the small, irregular shell fragments could perform well beneath asphalt pavements. The next experiment moved the research outside the confines of the laboratory. Rather than depend only on the results of laboratory testing on samples, the engineers were able to see the performance of the material after the road had been built.The researchers used a falling weight deflectometer to measure how much the road surface bent under a controlled load, helping them assess the pavement’s strength without digging into it. The Society of Materials Science, Japan also reports that maximum deflection at the loading point tended to decrease during the monitoring period, suggesting the pavement resisted bending more effectively under the test conditions. The best results came from the section containing nearly dried oyster-shell fragments, where the estimated California Bearing Ratio (CBR), a measure of soil strength and resistance to penetration, exceeded the target set for ground improvement.These findings suggested that oyster-shell fragments could be a useful alternative in the road-widening project, but they did not establish that shell powder or other forms of oyster-shell material could replace conventional road materials in every situation. Further testing under different soil and weather conditions, along with longer-term monitoring, would be needed to determine how well the material performed over time.The significance of the Japanese study lay in its practical approach to waste management. Rather than sending discarded oyster shells for disposal, the researchers tested whether the material could serve a useful purpose in road construction. The 70-metre trial produced encouraging results for the ground supporting the pavement, but it did not establish that oyster shells could be used directly as a road-surfacing material. The study also did not quantify the long-term cost savings or establish how the material would perform under different conditions over many years. Nevertheless, it showed that locally available shell waste could meet a specific ground-improvement target under the conditions tested.The March 2002 project provided a field-based assessment of oyster-shell fragments as a construction material, moving beyond the idea of waste reuse to examine their performance under real road conditions. Its findings offered evidence for a potential use in areas with substantial quantities of discarded shells, while leaving questions about durability, wider applications and long-term economic benefits unresolved.
Article Summary: Researchers in Japan explored the application of crushed oyster shells for enhancing the structural integrity of roads in a widening project. Researchers monitored the road’s response to traffic using pavement deflection measurements and found that deflection decreased over time. The study suggested that the small, irregular shell fragments could perform well beneath asphalt pavements.

Article Title: YouTuber Matt Walsh sounds ‘grim’ warning about AI chatbots as he questions what happens when humans replace friends
Article Text:
YouTuber Matt Walsh sounds ‘grim’ warning about AI chatbots as he questions what happens when humans replace friends

Matt Walsh Questions the Growing Bond Between Young People and AI Chatbots

Matt Walsh Has Also Raised Concerns About AI Taking Jobs and Changing Creative Work

What Can Robots Do?

Conservative commentator Matt Walsh has raised concerns about young people turning to artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for regular conversations and emotional support. In a post on X on October 14, 2026, Walsh questioned what could happen if people began spending much of their day talking to AI instead of building connections with other people. His comments followed a post describing a passenger who asked ChatGPT a simple question about bringing Cava on a flight but then became deeply involved in a conversation with the chatbot.Walsh shared his concerns after reposting a post from the X account @normalboy. The original post described a passenger asking ChatGPT whether he could bring Cava, a fast-casual restaurant chain, onto a flight. The passenger then became involved in a longer conversation with the chatbot.For Walsh, the incident pointed to a bigger concern about how people use AI in their daily lives. He argued that some young people already treat chatbots like friends and spend long periods talking to them.“We need to face the fact that there’s already a huge number of people, especially younger people, who talk to AI like it’s their friend and carry on near-constant conversations with it.What happens when a critical mass of people spend most of their day bonding and communicating with an inhuman algorithm controlled by a trillion-dollar tech company? Nobody knows. Most of the dystopian sci-fi writers never even envisioned a scenario this bleak. And our leaders have apparently no interest in trying to prevent any of this from happening. Really grim stuff,” Walsh wrote on X.His main concern was not simply that people were using AI tools. Instead, he questioned what might happen if people began relying on chatbots for companionship and regular conversations. He also raised concerns about the power of large technology companies that develop and control these systems.Walsh did not provide evidence showing how many young people have formed close bonds with AI chatbots. His post instead expressed concern about a possible future in which these interactions become a major part of everyday life.Walsh's latest comments follow earlier criticism of AI and its growing role in society. He has questioned its possible effects on jobs, human relationships, and creative industries, including film, music, and advertising.On October 8, Walsh reacted to research published by Anthropic on September 30. The report, titled, examined the physical tasks robots could perform and the potential effect of combining robotics with large language models. The findings discussed the difference between tasks technology could perform and those it could carry out at a competitive cost.Walsh used the research to question whether technology companies should have so much influence over changes that could affect millions of workers. He argued that people had little say in how these technologies might reshape their lives.He has also criticized AI-generated entertainment. In December 2025, he spoke out against McDonald's AI-generated Christmas advertisement, questioning its artistic value. The production studio defended the project, saying human creators had spent weeks developing prompts and refining the shots.Walsh also criticized AI-generated music, arguing that computer-made songs could threaten human creativity. His objections extend beyond whether AI can produce realistic images or music. He has questioned whether technology can replace the human experiences and creative choices that give art its meaning.His October 14 post returned to another part of the debate: how AI might affect people's relationships. While chatbots can answer questions and hold conversations, Walsh questioned what could happen if people increasingly treated them as substitutes for human connection. His post raised that concern without establishing what the long-term effects of such relationships will be.
Article Summary: Conservative commentator Matt Walsh has raised concerns about young people turning to AI chatbots for regular conversations and emotional support. Walsh questioned what could happen if people began spending much of their day talking to AI instead of building connections with other people. His comments followed a post describing a passenger who asked ChatGPT a simple question about bringing Cava on a flight.

Article Title: In 2024, Lancashire friends outgrew a small gaming shed and built a £2,000-plus replacement from scratch with an 18-foot table and a memorial to a friend; two years later, it won Britain's Shed of the
Article Text:
The shed features an 18-foot gaming table, storage for equipment and miniatures, and a tea-making station.

Inside Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0

Building shed amid Scott's illness

Britain's Shed of the Year

A garden shed built by a group of friends in Lancashire for their tabletop gaming sessions has won Britain's 2026 Shed of the Year competition. Known as Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0, the building belongs to Chris Otterburn and serves as a meeting place for friends who share an interest in wargaming. It also contains a memorial to their friend Scott Forrest, who died of cancer before the shed was completed.The shed was named the overall winner of the competition's 20th edition. According to Shedworking, the project was built with help from Chris's friends while Scott was undergoing cancer treatment. Although Scott could not see the finished building, the group included a dedicated space to remember him.The shed was entered into the competition by Chris's friend Dave, rather than Chris himself. Dave believed that Chris would not have submitted the project on his own or spoken openly about the amount of work that had gone into building it.The finished shed includes an 18-foot gaming table, storage areas for gaming equipment and miniature figures, and a station for making tea. The friends continue to meet there every week, using the space for their hobby while keeping Scott's memory alive.Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 was designed primarily for wargaming which is a tabletop hobby in which participants use miniature figures and specially prepared boards to play simulated battles.The group needed a dedicated space where they could set up their games, keep their equipment and meet regularly.The building has an 18-foot table at its centre, providing room for the group's gaming activities. It also has storage for battle boards and miniature figures that the friends have painted themselves. The painting work takes place in a separate shed, allowing the main building to be used for gaming sessions. Another feature is a tea-making station.Dave, who entered the shed into the competition, explained why he wanted the project to receive recognition. "Chris would never have entered it himself. He’d also never admit just how much work has gone into creating it or how much it means to all of us. It’s become somewhere we meet every week, enjoy our hobby, make endless cups of tea and remember our friend Scott,” he said, as quoted by Shedworking.The construction of the shed was a group effort. Chris's friends helped with the work while Scott Forrest, one of their fellow gaming enthusiasts, was receiving treatment for cancer.Scott died before the building could be completed, so the group decided to include a memorial area for him inside the finished shed.For Chris, the recognition was particularly meaningful because the project involved several friends and had become closely connected with Scott's memory.“Winning Shed of the Year is an incredible honour and means so much to everyone who’s been part of this journey. What started as a hobby project has become somewhere our friends can come together every week, enjoy our shared passion and remember Scott. It’s far more than just a shed, and knowing other people have connected with our story makes this award incredibly special,” he said.The 2026 competition marked the 20th year of Shed of the Year, which recognises garden buildings created for different purposes across the UK.Andrew Wilcox, the competition's founder and head judge, said the quality of entries had been particularly strong this year. However, Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 stood out not only because of its construction but also because of the story behind it.“Otty’s Hobby Shed 2.0 perfectly captures what Shed of the Year is all about. It’s an outstanding build, but it was the story behind it that made it our overall winner,” Wilcox said.He added that the shed demonstrated how a garden building could become a place for maintaining friendships, preserving memories and enjoying shared interests.
Article Summary: Otty's Hobby Shed 2.0 features an 18-foot gaming table, storage for equipment and miniatures, and a tea-making station. It also contains a memorial to their friend Scott Forrest, who died of cancer before the shed was completed.

Article Title: Britain built a 70-foot water tower disguised as a house in 1923; its 50,000-gallon tank was damaged by a wartime shell before the landmark became a holiday home
Article Text:
Representative Image of Thorpeness’s whimsical house-shaped water tower surrounded by trees in Suffolk ( AI Generrated Image)

House in the Clouds: how Thorpeness disguised a water tower

Wartime damage changed the water tower’s capacity

From water infrastructure to holiday accommodation

In the English village of Thorpeness, a 70-foot structure built to store water was designed to resemble a house perched above the trees. Completed in 1923, the building concealed a tank with an original capacity of 50,000 gallons, while the structure below provided living accommodation. Known as the House in the Clouds, it was part of the development of Thorpeness, a planned holiday village on the Suffolk coast. Glencairn Stuart Ogilvie, the owner and developer of the Thorpeness Estate, conceived the village and commissioned architects to help realise its distinctive design. Historic England credits Frederick Forbes Glennie with the building’s 1923 design, commissioned as part of Glencairn Stuart Ogilvie’s development of Thorpeness. Its timber weatherboarding, gabled roof and domestic-style windows helped it fit the village’s unusual architectural character. More than a century later, the building remains a landmark, despite no longer serving its original purpose as a water tower. Its survival shows how a practical structure, shaped by whimsy and later adapted for new uses, can become the defining landmark of a planned village’s character.The House in the Clouds was built to provide a water supply for Thorpeness. Its unusual appearance reflected the character of the village, which Ogilvie developed as a holiday destination with buildings designed to create a distinctive landscape rather than a conventional resort. The building’s Historic England listing describes a steel-frame structure clad in weatherboarding, topped by a pantiled, gabled roof. The lower part consists of a five-storey tower, while the upper section, supported by arched corner braces, housed the water tank. Windows were incorporated into the structure, including casement windows and projecting bay windows.The original tank held 50,000 gallons. According to the property’s official history, water was pumped from a well using the neighbouring windmill, with a petrol engine available as an alternative when wind conditions were insufficient. The elevated tank formed part of the water-supply system developed for the village. The building was initially called the Gazebo. Mrs Malcolm Mason, a children’s author and friend of Ogilvie, christened it the House in the Clouds. The property’s history records that a poem she wrote in 1923 was inspired by the building. Its new name captured the appearance of a house seemingly suspended above the surrounding trees. Historic England, which designated the building Grade II listed in 1995, describes it as a landmark and the best-known building in the resort village. Its combination of domestic architecture and water-storage infrastructure has helped preserve its distinctive identity.The building was damaged during the Second World War. According to the property’s official history, an English Bofors anti-aircraft shell passed through the tank’s south-eastern corner in 1943 while the gun was firing at a V1 flying bomb. The shell damaged the tank, and two women, the Miss Humphreys, were occupying the accommodation below and were asleep at the time. The subsequent repairs reduced the tank’s capacity from 50,000 gallons to 30,000 gallons. The property’s history records that sections of the tank’s existing steel were used in the repair. The reduction meant that the tower could hold 20,000 fewer gallons than it had originally been designed to store.The building’s water-supply arrangements also evolved over the following decades. An electric pump replaced the petrol engine in 1953, according to the property’s history. By 1963, a wider water supply had been introduced to the area, although the tank continued to be used for storage for a period afterwards. The tower eventually ceased to serve its original function. The property’s history places the end of its use for local water storage in 1977. The tank itself was removed in 1979, opening the way for the former storage space to become part of the house. Refurbishment of the interior and restoration of the garden began in 1987. These changes allowed the structure to survive beyond the purpose for which it had been built. Rather than remaining a working water tower, it became a house whose unusual upper section no longer needed to accommodate a large volume of water.Today, the House in the Clouds operates as holiday accommodation. Its official accommodation page lists five bedrooms distributed across the second, third and fourth floors, with a games room on the fifth floor. The different levels allow guests to experience a building whose layout developed from its original combination of a water tank and living space. The property stands on Uplands Road in Thorpeness, in Suffolk, close to the village’s golf course and Meare, the artificial lake created as part of the resort’s development. Visitors can find practical details through the property’s official location page.The building’s appeal comes from the contrast between its appearance and its original function. From a distance, its roof and weatherboarded exterior resemble a house elevated above the village. Its history, however, is tied to a practical need: storing and supplying water to the developing community. The House in the Clouds is an example of how infrastructure can become part of a place’s architectural identity. Built in 1923, damaged during wartime, altered when its water-storage role ended, and later adapted for holiday use, it has remained a recognisable feature of Thorpeness. Its original purpose has disappeared, but the structure continues to serve a new one while retaining the appearance that made it unusual in the first place.
Article Summary: The House in the Clouds was part of the development of Thorpeness, a planned holiday village on the Suffolk coast. Completed in 1923, the building concealed a tank with an original capacity of 50,000 gallons, while the structure below provided living accommodation. Its timber weatherboarding, gabled roof and domestic-style windows helped it fit the village's unusual architectural character.

Article Title: British prop maker spends £9,000 building a backyard spaceship with a bar, seating that doubles as a bed and a screen showing distant planets
Article Text:
PC: AI Generated

How Chester Walsh turned his backyard into a Star Wars-inspired spaceship

Building the spaceship took three months and around £9,000

Star Wars-inspired design of Chester Walsh’s garden spaceship

How Chester Walsh made his backyard spaceship a functional social space

The backyard spaceship attracted millions of online views

A friend ended up spending the night inside

A British prop maker has turned a corner of his backyard into a science-fiction hideaway, complete with a bar, curved seating that doubles as a bed and a screen showing distant planets. In an interview with PEOPLE, Chester Walsh, 29, spent three months building the spaceship-inspired retreat at his home in Northamptonshire, with the project costing around £9,000. A lifelong fan of science fiction and comic books, he drew on several familiar spacecraft designs to shape the exterior and interior. What began as a personal project during renovations soon attracted millions of views online, giving Walsh a chance to showcase his craft while creating an unusual place to spend evenings with friends.Walsh, 29, has long been interested in science fiction and comic books, with the Star Wars universe providing much of the visual inspiration for his work. Before building the spacecraft, he had already experimented with transforming ordinary garden structures. At a previous home, he converted part of an old shed into a tiki bar and decorated a garden cabin used as an office and gym with science-fiction-inspired wall panels.The new project gave him an opportunity to take those ideas further. Renovation work at his house had temporarily left his usual workshop unavailable, so a substantial outdoor build offered a way to keep working while developing his portfolio. He wanted something that looked like a spacecraft but could also function as a comfortable place to spend time with friends.Rather than copying a recognisable ship in its entirety, Walsh combined details from several fictional spacecraft and other science-fiction settings. He researched reference images and prepared three-dimensional models before construction began. The overall shape drew inspiration from the Intersystem Transport at Star Wars: Galaxy's Edge, while the interior would incorporate familiar elements from other parts of the franchise.The construction started with the less glamorous work of preparing the ground. Walsh excavated the site, laid a sub-base and arranged for a reinforced concrete foundation to be poured. He then worked with the glamping pod company Made of Bits to develop a timber frame to his specifications.The structure rests on approximately 100 pedestal supports. As well as allowing air to circulate beneath it, the arrangement helps give the building the appearance of hovering above the ground. Walsh covered the frame with 6mm plywood and a waterproof EPDM rubber membrane before shaping the exterior with EVA foam and adding fibreglass for strength and weather protection.Most of the work was completed by Walsh himself. A registered electrician was brought in to run an armoured cable to the building and connect the electrical fittings and lights he had installed. His experience making props and working alongside his father, a builder, gave him a useful foundation, although the project still presented unfamiliar challenges.The budget had also grown beyond his initial hopes. Walsh originally set himself a ceiling of £10,000, while aiming to keep spending below £7,000. Once the concrete work, timber frame, fibreglass, electrical work, an interior monitor and numerous trips to the DIY retailer Wickes were included, the materials and construction costs came to roughly £9,000.Inside, Walsh used wood, Foamex, foam panels, paint and decorative finishes to create an environment that felt distinct from an ordinary garden room. The design took considerable inspiration from the Millennium Falcon as it appeared in Solo: A Star Wars Story, when the spacecraft belonged to Lando Calrissian rather than Han Solo.That version of the ship appealed to Walsh because of its cleaner appearance. The influence can be seen in the oval doorway and the panels surrounding it, as well as the ceiling, where white sections with rounded edges contrast with a black background. Elements inspired by Ahsoka Tano's spacecraft also feature around the entrance.The curved seating booth is another central part of the design. It follows the shape of the interior and provides a place for guests to sit together, rather than dividing the space into rows of separate seats. It is also long enough for one person to sleep on, making it possible to use the spacecraft as an occasional overnight retreat.Other details come from different corners of the science-fiction world. Walsh looked to the Death Star for lighting ideas and drew on the design of Disney's former Star Wars: Galactic Starcruiser when choosing the flooring.The spaceship was designed to serve a practical purpose alongside its decorative one. A small bar provides storage for drinks, with a table Walsh found on Facebook Marketplace fitting the setting well enough to become part of the finished interior.Walsh recessed a monitor behind the wall panels and positioned it to line up with a false windshield. Footage of outer space and distant planets plays on the screen, giving visitors the impression that they are looking out from inside a spacecraft. The effect helps connect the different elements of the room. Without the screen, the curved seating, lighting and futuristic panels would still establish the theme, but the moving images give the apparent window a function beyond decoration.Walsh said, “My favorite feature is probably the oval doorway and surrounding paneling overall.” Visitors, however, have tended to respond to the whole structure rather than singling out one particular detail. Friends and family were familiar with his enthusiasm for ambitious projects, so their reactions were generally positive rather than surprised by the idea itself.One neighbour helped him excavate the foundation and later returned to see the completed build, taking photographs and videos. Another stopped by for a cup of tea and was impressed by the result.Walsh intended to document the construction from the beginning. Sharing the process offered a way to develop his social media presence, but he also hoped that showing what he could make might bring new customers and professional opportunities.As reported by the PEOPLE, He published more than 19 instalments following the build, covering the project from its foundations through to the completed interior. The detailed videos gave viewers a closer look at the work involved, including the practical decisions and techniques that went into shaping the structure.According to Walsh, the project has accumulated more than 2.5 million views across social media. The response also created a steady stream of questions from people curious about the construction, costs and materials.Rather than trying to respond individually to every comment, he points viewers towards the original series, which contains more detail about the different stages. Some people have told him that seeing the project encouraged them to try their own smaller-scale spaceship-inspired garden buildings.The attention has given the project a life beyond the original plan, although its main purpose remains personal. Walsh wanted a place where friends could gather without everyone having to stay in the house. If one group was talking indoors, another could spend time in the spacecraft.The room has already been used for evenings with friends, including one occasion that demonstrated why Walsh had made the seating long enough to serve as a bed. After a few drinks, one friend decided to sleep inside the spaceship. Walsh discovered the following morning that he had gone through with it, spending the night curled up on the curved booth while the monitor continued displaying images of outer space.For Walsh, the incident was funny but also a satisfying demonstration of what he had intended to create. The structure was not meant to be a static prop that could only be admired from the garden. It was built to be occupied, with room for people to sit, talk, have a drink and, if the evening lasted long enough, stay overnight.
Article Summary: Chester Walsh, 29, spent three months building the spaceship-inspired retreat at his home in Northamptonshire. A lifelong fan of science fiction and comic books, he drew on several familiar spacecraft designs to shape the exterior and interior. The design took considerable inspiration from the Millennium Falcon as it appeared in Solo: A Star Wars Story.

Article Title: In cigarette-butt asphalt tests, researchers found a 1.5% filter-waste blend gave the mix its best resistance to permanent deformation
Article Text:
The work examined cigarette butts as a waste material that could be incorporated into bituminous road mixtures | Wikimedia Commons

The 1.5% mix behaved differently under load

Researchers first tested cigarette-butt contents of 1%, 3% and 5% in the 2018 experiment | Wikimedia Commons

Researchers have tested several ways to use the waste

Researchers have tested cigarette-butt waste as an ingredient in asphalt mixtures, with one study finding that a mix that contained 1.5% cigarette butts had the lowest flow value among the tested concentrations, which indicates the strongest resistance to deformation by that measure. The same study found that increasing the cigarette-butt content changed the mixture's behavior under load, although its separate high-temperature rutting test produced a different optimum.The work examined cigarette butts as a waste material that could be incorporated into bituminous road mixtures, and researchers prepared samples with different amounts of cigarette butts and measured properties including Marshall stability, flow and resistance to deformation. Most conventional filters are made from cellulose acetate, which is a form of plastic-like cellulose that does not readily break down in the environment. Cigarette butts that have been used can also contain residual tobacco, tar and other substances, which has made their disposal an environmental problem. A later review of cigarette-butt asphalt research noted that researchers have investigated several ways of encapsulating or incorporating the waste into pavement materials.Researchers first tested cigarette-butt contents of 1%, 3% and 5% in the 2018 experiment, and the 3% mixture produced serious segregation, so the researchers tested lower concentrations of 1%, 1.5% and 2%. The Marshall test was then used to assess the mixtures, following which researchers reported that the 1.5% mixture had the lowest flow value among the tested cigarette-butt concentrations. In asphalt testing, flow is related to the amount of deformation that occurs under the Marshall loading conditions, and the paper therefore identified 1.5% as the best proportion for anti-deformation performance based on that measurement.In another study, the researchers examined high-temperature performance using a wheel-tracking or rutting test, and the dynamic stability increased as the cigarette-butt content increased, with the 2% mixture recording the highest dynamic stability in that experiment. “Best resistance to deformation” can refer to different measurements, as the 1.5% result came from the flow-value comparison, while the 2% result came from the high-temperature dynamic-stability test, and the study did not establish that 1.5% was universally the optimum concentration for every form of pavement deformation.One investigation that was published in Construction and Building Materials examined cigarette butts that were encapsulated in bitumen before they were incorporated into stone mastic asphalt. That research found improved Marshall stability in mixtures that contained 1% and 2% encapsulated cigarette butts and reported increased resistance to permanent deformation, which is important because cigarette filters can contain substances that may leach out. The researchers therefore also examined leachate from the asphalt mixtures rather than treating the waste simply as an inert filler.A larger review of waste fibres in asphalt has since placed cigarette-butt materials among several experimental additives that are being investigated for pavement applications. The research has included whole cigarette butts encapsulated in asphalt, shredded filter fibres and other processed forms, with different studies having used different concentrations and testing methods, so their results cannot simply be combined into one recommended percentage.The 1.5% finding therefore belongs to a specific laboratory study and a specific performance measurement, and it does not mean that roads containing exactly 1.5% cigarette-butt waste have been proven to outperform conventional asphalt in real-world traffic. The research instead shows that a small proportion of cigarette-butt waste can alter the mechanical behavior of an asphalt mixture under controlled testing.
Article Summary: Researchers have tested cigarette-butt waste as an ingredient in asphalt mixtures. One study found that a mix that contained 1.5% cigarette butts had the lowest flow value among the tested concentrations. A separate high-temperature rutting test produced a different optimum. The research shows that a small proportion of waste can alter the mechanical behavior of an asphalt mixture.

Article Title: In 1991, California’s Oakland fire left 1,272 pets affected; researchers found that ID collars made pets more than 10 times as likely to be reunited with their owners
Article Text:
Representative AI image of rescued pets wearing identification collars as searchers look for animals separated from their homes after a devastating wildfire. Image credits: ChatGPT.

A fire left hundreds of pets without their owners

The simple collar that made a remarkable difference

Firefighters spray water along the edge of a burnout operation during the Creek Fire in California. Credits - Wikipedia

Why the lesson still matters

When a wildfire tears through a neighbourhood, people may have only minutes to get out. Pets may flee in panic, hide in unfamiliar places, or become separated from their owners during evacuations. Even after the flames are extinguished, finding these animals can take weeks or months. A fire that swept through Oakland, California, in October 1991 showed how a collar with an owner’s name and address could greatly improve a pet’s chances of getting home.According to a 1998 study published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association , the 1991 Oakland fire left many cats and dogs missing, abandoned or roaming without their owners. Researchers analysed records for 1,075 cats and 197 dogs affected by the fire. They found that pets wearing collars with their owners’ names and addresses were more than ten times as likely to be reunited with their families as pets without collars.The fire erupted on 19 October 1991 and quickly spread in the Oakland-Berkeley hills. Most people were away from home when the fire struck, and road closures and evacuation restrictions made it hard for many to return and collect their pets.Some pets escaped, while others were left behind in the chaos. The study evaluated data collected by the Oakland Firestorm Pet Hotline between 1991 and 1995. The study sample included 1,075 cats and 197 dogs affected by the fire, for a total of 1,272 pets. The researchers also evaluated data from 221 cats and 128 dogs that were not affected by the disaster.The hotline did more than take phone calls; it also recorded reports of missing and found animals. Most of the animals found after the disaster were either stray pets or animals already living ferally in the area. Some animals remained missing, and the researchers assumed they had died in the disaster. It was therefore difficult to determine whether all the animals recorded as found had been separated from their families by the fire. Research states that the hotline activity peaked on the third and fourth days after the disaster, before calls declined and levelled off by the 21st day.The study produced several findings, but one stood out. Animals wearing collars with their owners’ names and addresses were more than ten times as likely to be reunited with their owners as animals without collars. The reason is straightforward. A pet may be found by a passerby or rescuer who can identify the owner only from the tag.Identification alone did not guarantee a reunion. The longer owners waited to search, the less likely they were to reunite with their pets. After the disaster, time mattered because animals could wander off or be adopted before owners found them. Nevertheless, the results sent a clear message to pet owners. Pets should be identified before a disaster, because there may be no time to do it afterwards. A collar with current contact information can help a finder reach the owner quickly.The Oakland fire highlighted the difficulties of reuniting animals with their owners during an emergency. Some animals were adopted by the people who found them, particularly those discovered near the fire zone. The incident also underlined the importance of pet identification, both in everyday life and during disasters.Collars and tags can help rescuers identify a pet quickly, although they may become lost or detached. Microchips provide an additional means of identification, provided the animal is scanned and the registered contact details are up to date. Using both visible identification and a registered microchip therefore offers a more reliable way to reconnect lost pets with their owners.As the Oakland study drew on records from a single disaster, its findings should not be assumed to apply equally to every fire or evacuation. Nevertheless, the practical lesson remains relevant: clear, accessible identification can improve the chances of reuniting lost animals with their families, particularly when an emergency separates them.
Article Summary: The 1991 Oakland fire left many cats and dogs missing, abandoned or roaming without their owners. Researchers analysed records for 1,075 cats and 197 dogs affected by the fire. They found that pets wearing collars with their owners’ names and addresses were more than ten times as likely to be reunited with their families as pets without collars.

Article Title: A Vermont forester bought 175 acres of degraded woodland in 2017; after nine years of restoring habitats, the land now features a wildlife pond, rich vegetation and an orchard of more than 100 fruit t
Article Text:
How a Vermont forester spent nine years restoring a damaged forest

He turned a rubbish-filled clearing into a pond

Rich vegetation and an orchard of more than 100 fruit trees

A conservation easement protects the property

How Ethan Tapper shared his experience

Vermont forester Ethan Tapper bought 175 acres of degraded woodland in Bolton, Vermont, in 2017 and began restoring its ecosystem. The property, which he named Bear Island, had been affected by decades of logging, invasive plant growth and soil erosion. Over the following years, Tapper selectively cut trees, removed invasive vegetation, planted acorns and repaired damage left by earlier land use. He also transformed a rubbish-filled clearing into a pond, where frogs and salamanders appeared within months. The woodland now features a diverse forest understory, habitat for several bird species and an orchard containing more than 100 fruit trees. His work has turned the property into a long-term conservation project focused on improving forest health and habitat diversity.When Tapper acquired Bear Island, the property reflected its history as pastureland and a woodlot. Earlier logging had removed many healthy trees, leaving behind diseased and poorly formed growth. Eroded logging roads crossed the land, while a clearing once used for timber storage was littered with rubbish.Tapper began by selectively removing trees to give healthier specimens more room to grow. He also cleared diseased beech trees, stabilised eroding trails and planted tens of thousands of acorns to encourage future forest growth.His approach combines tree management with efforts to improve the woodland's overall structure. A 2025 profile by forestry equipment manufacturer Tigercat described around 30 acres of regenerating forest with a diverse understory among the results of his work.One of the most visible changes at Bear Island involved a clearing previously used to store timber. Tapper and a friend rented an excavator and dug a pond, replacing a rubbish-filled area with a water feature.The pond is approximately 20 feet deep and about half the length of a football field. According to Audubon, frogs and salamanders appeared within months of its creation, adding amphibians to the wildlife associated with the recovering property.The woodland now supports a varied understory, including bracken and several fern species. These plants grow beneath the main forest canopy, contributing to the diversity of vegetation across the property.Tapper has also established an orchard containing more than 100 fruit trees. Alongside the pond and regenerating woodland, the orchard adds another distinct feature to the landscape.Birds recorded on the property include American redstarts, veeries, black-throated blue warblers and mourning warblers, according to Audubon. In 2023, Tapper became one of Audubon's first endorsed foresters in Vermont. The programme promotes forest-management practices designed to support birds and other wildlife.In 2022, Tapper donated a conservation easement on Bear Island, placing permanent legal protections on the land. Such agreements restrict certain uses of a property to preserve its conservation value.The easement extends the project's long-term impact by helping safeguard the woodland beyond Tapper's ownership. It complements the practical work carried out on the property by providing a legal framework for its continued protection.Tapper documented his work in his 2024 book, How to Love a Forest: The Bittersweet Work of Tending a Changing World. Drawing on his experience at Bear Island, the book explores forest ecology and the decisions involved in managing woodland.Through articles, talks and social media, Tapper also explains how forestry practices can influence ecosystem health. His work highlights the role of selective cutting, invasive-species management and habitat improvement in caring for forests affected by earlier land use.Nearly nine years after purchasing Bear Island, Tapper continues to manage the woodland and its orchard. The pond, diverse vegetation and regenerating forest reflect the results of sustained work on a landscape once heavily altered by logging and other human activities.
Article Summary: Vermont forester Ethan Tapper bought 175 acres of degraded woodland in Bolton, Vermont, in 2017 and began restoring its ecosystem. The property, which he named Bear Island, had been affected by decades of logging, invasive plant growth and soil erosion. Over the following years, Tapper selectively cut trees, removed invasive vegetation, planted acorns and repaired damage left by earlier land use. He also transformed a rubbish-filled clearing into a pond, where frogs and salamanders appeared within months.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.
